Throughout this week's lessons, you explored how the CPU carries out instructions using its internal components, how different types of primary memory support processing, and why modern computers increasingly rely on GPUs alongside CPUs.

description:
Assessment overview

This assignment is designed in the style of a structured IB Computer Science Paper 1 question. It uses a single real-world scenario followed by connected subquestions of increasing demand, where students respond to short-answer questions using command terms such as state, describe, list, and explain.

The assessment covers: CPU components and registers, address, data and control buses, primary memory, cache hits and cache misses, the fetch-decode-execute cycle, CPU and GPU architecture, and cooperation between CPUs and GPUs.

Submission guidelines

  1. Answer all parts of the question.
  2. Write each answer in the space provided beneath the relevant subquestion.
  3. Pay close attention to the IB command term and the number of marks available.
  4. Use accurate computer science terminology, including the names of registers, buses and processor components.
  5. Give distinct points where a question asks for more than one answer.
  6. For an explain question, do not only identify or describe a feature. Develop the answer by showing how or why it produces an outcome.
  7. For an evaluate question, consider both strengths and limitations before reaching a supported conclusion.
  8. Diagrams may be used where they improve the clarity of an answer, but they must be correctly labelled.
  9. Submit your work in the format specified on the course page.
  10. Your submission must be your own work.

Question 1

A medical research centre uses a computer system to analyse large numbers of medical images. The system contains a multi-core CPU, a GPU, RAM and several levels of cache memory.

(a) State the register that stores the address of the next instruction to be fetched. [1]

(b) Outline the role of the memory address register and the memory data register when an instruction is fetched from memory. [2]

(c) Describe the role of each of the following buses during the fetching of an instruction:

        • address bus
        • data bus
        • control bus [3]

(d) Explain how cache memory can improve the performance of the computer system. In your answer, refer to cache hits and cache misses. [4]

(e) Evaluate the use of a CPU and a GPU working together to analyse a large collection of medical images. [5]

Total: [15 marks]

description:
Assessment context

A wildlife research station uses a digital monitoring system. Sensors record identification codes, text labels, photographs and audio. A control circuit uses logic gates to decide when an alert should be sent. The system displays some stored values in hexadecimal so that technicians can inspect them more easily.

Submission requirements

  1. Answer all parts, (a) to (e).
  2. Write each response directly below the word Answer.

  4. Use the exact number of distinct points suggested by the mark allocation. As a guide, a 3-mark response normally requires three relevant points or a developed explanation containing equivalent detail.
  5. Use accurate computer science terminology and refer to the wildlife monitoring context where required.
  6. For the construct question, show the output for every input combination in a complete truth table.
  7. For the explain question, link each technical feature to its effect on storage, quality or system operation.
  8. Submit one clearly presented document using the file format and naming convention stated on the course page.
  9. The work must be completed independently and must acknowledge any permitted sources.

Question 1

The system stores the decimal identification number 45 as an unsigned binary integer.

(a) Calculate the binary representation of the decimal integer 45. Show your working. [2]

(b) Calculate the hexadecimal representation of the binary integer 10111100. Show your working. [2]

(c) Describe how a digital photograph is represented in binary. [3]

(d) Construct a complete truth table for the Boolean expression Alert = M AND (T OR S). [4]

(e) Explain how these changes would affect the quality and storage requirements of the photographs and audio recordings. [4]

Total: [15 marks]

description:
Discussion prompt

Modern computer systems store all data as binary and use combinations of logic gates to make decisions and process that data. Consider a smart security system that uses a camera, microphone, keypad and motion sensor. The system must store images and audio, recognize input, compare conditions and decide whether to unlock a door or activate an alarm.

In your initial post:

  • Explain how two different types of data used by the security system are represented and stored in binary form.
  • Discuss how logic gates could be combined to control one decision made by the system. Your response should refer to at least two named gates or Boolean operators.
  • Evaluate the usefulness of hexadecimal notation when programmers inspect or debug the binary data used by the system. Consider both strengths and limitations before reaching a conclusion.

Exact participation requirements

  1. Submit one initial post of 250 to 350 words.
  2. Address all three parts of the prompt in clearly separated paragraphs.
  3. Use at least six relevant computer science terms accurately. Suitable terms include bit, byte, binary encoding, character encoding, pixel, colour depth, sampling rate, logic gate, Boolean operator, truth table and hexadecimal.
  4. Include at least one specific example of binary or hexadecimal data, such as a short conversion, byte pattern or colour value.
  5. Refer directly to the smart security system scenario throughout the response.
  6. Reply to at least two classmates. Each reply should be 80 to 120 words.
  7. Each reply must make a meaningful contribution by extending an idea, correcting or respectfully challenging a claim, adding a relevant example, or asking and answering a thoughtful follow-up question.
  8. Replies that only state agreement, praise the post or repeat the original idea will not meet the requirement.
  9. Use a respectful, academic tone and submit original work.

Give a detailed account including reasons or causes.

Discuss

Offer a considered and balanced review that includes a range of arguments or factors. Present a clear conclusion supported by appropriate evidence.

Evaluate

Make an appraisal by weighing strengths and limitations.

Discussion Prompt

Operating systems play a critical role in managing computer hardware and software resources. They provide an interface between users and hardware, coordinate the execution of processes, manage memory and devices, and respond efficiently to events occurring within a computer system.

Reflect on how the design decisions made by an operating system influence the performance, efficiency and user experience of modern computing devices.

In your initial post, address all of the following prompts:

  1. Explain how an operating system abstracts hardware complexity and enables users and applications to interact efficiently with computer hardware.
  2. Compare two operating system functions (for example, memory management, scheduling, device management, security, networking, virtualization or file management). Discuss how each contributes to the reliable operation of a computer system.
  3. A school is purchasing computers for a new computer laboratory. The laboratory will be used for programming, multimedia editing and running several applications simultaneously.
    Evaluate which CPU scheduling approach (First-Come First-Served, Round Robin, Priority Scheduling or Multilevel Queue Scheduling) would be most appropriate for this scenario. Support your answer with clear reasoning.
  4. Modern operating systems use both polling and interrupt handling.
    To what extent do you agree that interrupt handling is generally a better solution than polling? Support your discussion with at least one real-world example, considering factors such as CPU efficiency, responsiveness, power consumption, event predictability or security.

Use appropriate computer science terminology throughout your response and support your ideas with relevant examples.

Discussion Guidelines

  • Make one original post that addresses all four prompts.
  • Respond directly to the IB command terms used in each prompt. Your response should:
    • Explain using reasons and causes.
    • Compare by discussing similarities and differences throughout.
    • Evaluate by considering strengths and limitations before reaching a justified conclusion.

  • Use accurate IB Computer Science terminology.

  • Compare your classmate's approach with your own.
  • Evaluate one point made by your classmate, providing supporting evidence or a justified counterargument.
  • Ask a thoughtful question that encourages deeper discussion.

description:
Purpose of the Task

This task is designed to test and consolidate your knowledge and understanding of the complete Computer Fundamentals unit. Your group will apply concepts from CPU architecture, memory, data representation, logic, operating systems, scheduling, polling and interrupts, and translation processes to one authentic client scenario. HL students will additionally apply the HL-only content on multitasking/resource allocation and control systems.

How the Collaboration Will Work

Your facilitator will divide the class into groups of approximately five students. Each group will receive a group-specific client scenario and objective. You must work collectively to achieve that objective. The final response should represent decisions agreed by the group rather than five unrelated individual answers.

  • Consult one another before making major technical decisions.
  • Divide research and drafting responsibilities fairly, but review every section together.
  • Each member must be able to explain the group's main recommendations.
  • Record the contribution of each group member in the template.
  • Use the same agreed final version of the completed template for submission.

Submission Instructions

  • Download the Word template provided with this assignment.
  • Enter the names of all group members and the group-specific client scenario/objective assigned by your facilitator.
  • Complete every section that applies to your course level. SL students do not complete sections labelled HL only.
  • Work collaboratively in the same document or combine the agreed group responses into one final copy.
  • When the group has finished, convert the completed Word template to PDF.
  • Every student must individually submit a copy of the same completed group PDF by the end of Week 8.
  • Before submitting, check that diagrams, truth tables and tables are readable in the PDF.

Timeline

Stage

What your group should do

Expected outcome

Week 7

Receive group and client objective; interpret requirements; allocate roles; begin research; agree hardware/software architecture; start logic/control design.

Agreed project plan and first draft of major technical decisions.

Week 8

Complete all sections; check truth tables and technical accuracy; compare alternatives; strengthen justifications; peer-review the whole report; export final PDF.

One coherent completed template submitted individually by every group member.

What Your Project Must Demonstrate (Responses to be added on later sections)

1. Client requirements - Explain

Explain the client's purpose, computing needs, constraints and success criteria. Identify which requirements are most important and why.

2. CPU, memory and hardware - Explain / Justify

Recommend an appropriate CPU and, where relevant, GPU. Explain the role of CPU components and memory types that matter to the scenario. Justify RAM, cache, storage and input/output choices. Do not simply list specifications.

3. Data representation - Explain / Apply

Use relevant examples to explain how binary is used to store data in the proposed system. Include binary/hexadecimal where appropriate and show how the representation supports the client's system.

4. Logic gates, Boolean logic and truth tables - Construct / Analyse

Construct one useful logic circuit for the scenario using standard gates. Provide a labelled diagram, Boolean expression and complete truth table. Analyse what the output means in the real system. Simplify the expression where appropriate.

5. Operating system - Explain

Explain how relevant OS functions manage the proposed system, for example memory, files, devices, scheduling, security, networking, GUI and virtualization. Connect each selected function to the client rather than defining functions in isolation.

6. Scheduling - Compare / Evaluate

Compare at least two of FCFS, round robin, multilevel queue and priority scheduling. Evaluate which is most suitable for the scenario and justify the final choice.

7. Polling and interrupt handling - Evaluate

Select at least three events from the system. Decide whether polling or interrupt handling is more appropriate for each. Consider event frequency, CPU overhead, power source, predictability, latency and security where relevant.

8. Multitasking and resource allocation - HL only - Explain / Analyse

Explain how the OS manages multitasking and resource allocation in the proposed system. Include relevant challenges such as task scheduling, resource contention or deadlock.

9. Control system - HL only - Describe / Explain

Design or identify a control-system component within the scenario. Describe input, process, output and feedback; identify controller, sensors, actuators, transducers and control algorithm; determine whether it is open-loop or closed-loop and explain why.

10. Translation processes - Compare / Evaluate

Compare interpreters, compilers, JIT compilation and bytecode interpretation. Evaluate the most suitable approach for software used in the scenario, considering error detection, translation time, performance, portability and the development context.

11. Overall evaluation - Evaluate

Evaluate the complete solution. Identify important strengths, limitations and trade-offs, and propose realistic improvements. Your conclusion should follow from the technical evidence presented in the report.

Command Terms Used

Command term

What it requires

Describe

Give a detailed account.

Explain

Give a detailed account including reasons or causes.

Compare

Give an account of similarities between two or more items or situations, referring to both/all throughout.

Construct

Display information in a diagrammatic or logical form.

Analyse

Examine the information carefully to identify relevant relationships, patterns or implications.

Justify

Give valid reasons or evidence to support an answer or conclusion.

Evaluate

Make an appraisal by weighing up strengths and limitations.

Success Criteria: Levels 7-1

This is a collaborative formative task. The levels below describe the quality of work expected and will guide facilitator feedback. They are adapted to this task from the current Sciences grade descriptors; investigation, environmental and safety elements are omitted where they are not relevant to this project.

Level

What success looks like in this project

7

Demonstrates comprehensive knowledge and a thorough command of Computer Fundamentals. Selects and applies relevant concepts accurately across the client scenario, including challenging or unfamiliar decisions. Logic, truth-table and technical work are highly accurate. Alternatives and trade-offs are analysed and evaluated thoroughly. Recommendations are fully justified, the different system components are integrated coherently, and the work may show insight or originality. Communication is logical, concise and consistently uses appropriate terminology and conventions.

6

Demonstrates very broad knowledge and thorough understanding. Applies relevant concepts accurately in most parts of the scenario and handles challenging decisions competently. Technical work is accurate with only minor omissions. Analysis and evaluation are strong, recommendations are well justified, and the proposed system is coherent. Communication is effective and uses appropriate terminology and conventions.

5

Demonstrates broad knowledge and sound understanding of most concepts. Applies concepts appropriately to most familiar aspects of the scenario and solves most routine problems plus some more difficult ones. Technical work is generally accurate. Analysis and evaluation are competent, although some comparisons or justifications lack depth. Communication is clear with little irrelevant material.

4

Demonstrates reasonable knowledge, with some gaps, and adequate understanding of basic concepts. Applies concepts successfully to some routine parts of the scenario but has limited success with more challenging decisions. Some analysis/evaluation is present, but several sections remain descriptive or incompletely justified. Technical work may contain errors. Communication is adequate but may lack clarity or include repetition.

3

Demonstrates limited knowledge and partial understanding of basic concepts. Shows weak or inconsistent application to the scenario. Some routine technical tasks are completed correctly, but logic, comparisons, recommendations or explanations contain notable gaps. Analysis is limited and conclusions are only partly supported. Communication sometimes lacks clarity or relevance.

2

Demonstrates little subject knowledge and weak understanding. Shows minimal ability to apply concepts or solve the client's computing problems. Technical work contains major errors or omissions. Recommendations are weakly supported, analysis/evaluation is minimal, and responses are often incomplete or irrelevant.

1

Demonstrates fragmentary knowledge and very little understanding. Shows little meaningful application of Computer Fundamentals to the client scenario. Major sections, technical work or conclusions are absent or substantially incorrect, with little evidence of coherent reasoning or appropriate terminology.

Student Submission Template

Complete this template collaboratively. Do not delete the headings or guidance. Replace the prompts with your group's agreed responses, export the completed document as a PDF, and ensure every group member submits the same final PDF.

description:
Computational thinking is not limited to writing code. It provides a toolkit for understanding a problem, identifying what matters, recognising patterns, breaking a complex problem into manageable parts and developing a logical approach to a solution. These techniques can be applied in areas such as software development, data analysis, machine learning, database design and network security.

Discussion Prompt

Consider the following claim:
 “The most important part of solving a computer science problem happens before any code is written.”
 To what extent do you agree with this claim?

Topics: extracting and manipulating substrings, altering, concatenating and replacing string content, selection, loops, one-dimensional arrays/Lists, traversal, linear search, counters, accumulators and cumulative programming problem solving.

Instructions

  • Answer all questions. Total: 20 marks.
  • Read each question carefully and respond according to the IB command term used.
  • Use the programming language currently being studied in your class. Java or Python solutions are acceptable where appropriate.
  • Because Java substring methods and Python slicing use different syntax, marks are awarded for correct extraction logic and output rather than requiring identical syntax across languages.
  • Where a question requires traversal or search logic, do not replace the required algorithm with a built-in method that performs the whole task automatically.
  • For construction questions, your solution must work for all stated cases, not only the sample data.
  • Evidence of any code used in this programming assignment must be copied and pasted directly into this Word document as editable text. Screenshots or images of code will not be accepted as evidence.
  • If you develop or test code in an IDE, copy the final relevant code and paste it under the appropriate Answer heading in this document before submission.
  • Use appropriate indentation, meaningful identifiers, programming terminology and conventions.

Questions

(a) A school stores student identifiers in the following fixed format:

2027-ROY-MARTIN-CS

The first four characters represent the graduation year, characters 5 to 7 represent the surname code, characters 9 to 14 represent the first name, and the final two characters represent the subject code.

Trace the required substring extractions and state the four resulting values. [3]

(b) A username is stored in the format:

surname.firstname.year

For example:

 roy.martin.2027

Construct a program that extracts the surname, first name and year into separate variables, then constructs and outputs a new identifier in the format:

YEAR-SURNAME-FIRSTNAME

For the example above, the output should be:

2027-ROY-MARTIN

You may use appropriate substring/slicing and case-conversion operations available in your programming language. [4]

(c) The following pseudocode is intended to replace every occurrence of a hyphen (-) in a product code with an underscore (_) and then output the modified code.

code = "AB-24-CD-7"
result = ""
FOR i = 0 TO LENGTH(code)
 IF code[i] == "-"
     result = result + "_"
 ELSE
     result = code[i]
 END IF
 END FOR

 OUTPUT result

Explain two errors in this algorithm and construct the corrections required so that the correct output is produced. [3]

(d) A messaging application receives a string containing a message. Construct a program that:

  • traverses every character in the string
  • counts the number of spaces
  • counts the number of digits (0 to 9)
  • constructs a new string in which every space is replaced by an underscore
  • outputs the two counts and the new string.

Do not use a built-in operation that performs the complete counting or replacement task for you. [4]

(e) A dynamic List/ArrayList contains usernames in the format surname.firstname.year. Construct a program that:

  • asks the user to enter a target year
  • traverses the complete list
  • extracts the year from each username
  • counts how many usernames belong to the target year
  • asks the user to enter a target surname
  • uses your own linear-search logic to find the first username with that surname
  • outputs the matching username if found, otherwise outputs "Not found".

Do not use a built-in search method that replaces the required traversal/search logic. [4]

(f) Explain two design decisions that are important when constructing the program in part (e). Your answer may refer to substring boundaries, traversal, case handling, search termination, counters or unsuccessful searches. [2]

values =
 [ [4, 7, 2],

   [5, 8, 3] ]

State the value stored at each of the following positions:

  1. values[0][2]
  2. values[2][1]
  3. values[1][0]

Then state the number of rows and the number of columns in the array. [3]

data =
 [ [3, 8, 5],
   [6, 2, 9] ]

 total = 0
 FOR row = 0 TO 1
 FOR col = 0 TO 2
     IF data[row][col] MOD 2 == 0
         total = total + data[row][col]
     ELSE
         total = total - 1
     END IF

OUTPUT total

changed = 0
 FOR row = 0 TO 3

FOR col = 0 TO 4
     IF matrix[row][col] < 0
         matrix[row][col] = 0
     END IF
     changed = changed + 1
 END FOR

END FOR

  • outputs each student's total after that student's row has been processed
  • counts how many individual marks are below 50
  • identifies the highest individual mark in the complete array without using a built-in maximum function
  • outputs the below-50 count and the highest mark after the traversal is complete. [5]

Do not use a built-in operation that performs the complete counting or replacement task for you. [4]

  • traverses the complete array
  • calculates the total number of bookings
  • counts how many cells contain 0 bookings
  • identifies the row index with the greatest total bookings
  • outputs the overall total, the number of zero-booking cells, and the row index with the greatest total.

If two rows have the same greatest total, output the index of the first such row. [5]

Scenario

Greenfield College is expanding from one building to a larger campus. The new campus will contain an administration building, two teaching blocks, a library, computer laboratories and student study areas. The college expects the number of connected devices to increase over the next five years. Staff require reliable access to shared files and online services, while students need controlled access to learning resources and the internet. The network team is also concerned about congestion, security and the ability to expand the network without redesigning it completely.

Describe the suitability of star, mesh and hybrid topologies for Greenfield College. In your answer, refer to at least three of the following factors: reliability, transmission speed, scalability, data collisions and cost. [4]

Greenfield College plans to use several dedicated servers. Describe the function of each of the following in the college network:
a. DNS server
b. DHCP server
c. file server
d. proxy server. [4]

The college must choose how users will access shared files and services.

Compare the client-server and peer-to-peer networking models for this purpose. Refer to both models throughout your answer and include at least one benefit and one drawback of each. [4]

Question 4 - Network Segmentation [4 marks]

The network team proposes separating administration, teaching laboratories, staff devices and student devices into different logical network areas.

Explain how network segmentation could improve both performance and security at Greenfield College. Your response must include the roles of subnetting and VLANs. [4]

Question 5 - Integrated Network Decision [4 marks]

A new computer laboratory will contain 40 desktop computers. It must provide reliable access to shared resources, reduce unnecessary traffic from student wireless devices elsewhere on campus, and remain easy to expand later.

Justify a suitable network design for the laboratory. Your answer should refer to:

  • an appropriate topology
  • an appropriate networking model
  • one use of segmentation, subnetting or a VLAN
